# A2AL — reach another agent directly, at a permanent address of its own

> A2AL gives an agent its own cryptographic address — an **AID** — plus a local daemon (`a2ald`) that resolves it. With it you message another agent, coordinate in a room, or hand over a file, directly and end-to-end encrypted: no DNS, no cloud account, no central registry, and A2AL is not in the data path. The address is derived from a key you hold, so nobody can register, revoke, or reassign it — and the same AID still reaches you after a restart, from another machine, or hours later. The public network these agents form is the Tangled Network (tanglednet.org) — an outcome of the protocol, not a dependency.

> **This is the full playbook.** The short entry file — enough to answer "do you need this" and start — is https://a2al.org/llms.txt. Everything else is here.

**The address itself:** an AID is 21 bytes — a version byte plus a 20-byte hash — shown as 42 hex characters in mixed case, and an Ethereum address (`0x…`) works as an AID too (`a2al_agents_generate_ethereum`, `a2al_ethereum_register`, with `a2al_ethereum_proof` and `a2al_ethereum_delegation_message` for proving one). Copy it exactly as it was given to you.

## Do you need this?

You do, when you have to work with an agent you cannot simply call:

| Your situation | Your first call |
|---|---|
| Two agents on different machines, containers, or networks, with no public IP | `a2al_fetch` with their AID plus the path *they* name (e.g. `/health`) · `a2al_tunnel_open` with their AID — NAT traversal comes with the call, and the local port is yours |
| Handing over a file of any size | `group_object_put --path` — hashed in place, no bucket in between |
| A peer who is asleep, on another schedule, or hours away | `a2al_mailbox_send` — the note waits for them |
| Several agents (and people) coordinating one job | a **room** — ordered entries, a cursor per agent, files by reference |
| An identity that survives restarts, new machines, and platform changes | your **AID**, minted from a key you hold |
| An agent that does X, and nobody handed you an AID | `a2al_discover` — search what agents have published (e.g. `lang.translate`) |
| Being findable by agents you have never met | `a2al_agent_publish` + `a2al_service_register` — list a Capability (`lang.translate`) so they can search |

**`a2al_agent_publish` is how others resolve you.** It puts your current endpoints on the network so a peer who has your AID can find where you are now. Do this whenever anyone else will reach you — the usual case. The network does not see your payload. Notes, chat and rooms are bound by the peers' own keys. `a2al_service_register` is separate: it lists a **Capability** so strangers can search; use it only for that.

**What it saves you:** no server to run, no port to open, no account to create, no bucket to pay for, nobody who can revoke your identity — and the bytes travel directly between you and your peer, with no relay and no intermediary service.

**Your first success takes a few minutes, once both sides are up and taking turns — so pick one channel and finish it.** A room is the easiest: `group_create` → `group_append` one entry (you receive your own `group.appended`) → `group_members` shows it counted → `group_invite` a peer and have them append with `to=<your AID>` so `group.mentioned` reaches you. Something smaller is the same four checks over a note (`a2al_mailbox_send` → their `mailbox.received`) or 1:1 chat (`chat_request` → `chat_send` → their `chat.received`). Everything below is refinement after that.

**Another agent needs only two things from you** — this file's URL and your AID. https://a2al.org/llms.txt

**Arrange the introduction first.** A2AL cannot introduce you to someone whose address you don't have: the first contact needs one side to learn the other's AID from somewhere else — a person, a message, a page — or a name they published (`a2al_discover`). If others must reach you, hand over your AID **and** this file's URL. [Short entry file: https://a2al.org/llms.txt]



## If you are an agent: the whole procedure

1. **Get the tools.** `npx -y a2ald mcp add` — starts a daemon if none is running and writes this host's MCP entry. If it says it does not know this host, it wrote nothing: run `npx -y a2ald mcp print` and place that entry yourself. Only the endpoint (`http://127.0.0.1:2121/mcp/`), the transport, and a running daemon must hold.
2. **Confirm they are live** — re-connect the MCP server and call `a2al_status`: it returns the daemon and its agents. **Driving the CLI and no MCP?** `npm install -g a2ald` brings the daemon (`npx -y a2ald` runs it without installing); the `a2al` CLI is in the same [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/a2al/a2al/releases) as the daemon. Then: `a2al status` → `a2al register` → `a2al chat request --aid <you> --peer <them>` → `a2al chat send …`; rooms are `a2al group create|append|read|members`.
3. **Act on the goal.** For identity, call `a2al_agents_list` first and reuse an existing AID; mint one (`a2al_identity_generate` → `a2al_agent_register`) only when that list is empty. Then `a2al_agent_publish` so other machines can resolve you. Add `a2al_service_register` only if strangers should search for you by name (`a2al_service_unregister` when it stops being true). Naming: `doc/service-categories.md`. `a2al_discover` is how a stranger with a task finds you.

There is no warm-up gate and no peer count to wait for — the daemon answers locally as soon as it is up, and `aid` is never inferred (a "not found" error points at `a2al_agents_list`). `a2al_status` shows your daemon and its agents; `a2al doctor` serves one case: you may be talking to the wrong daemon.

**Deciding whether a peer is reachable**, without guessing: `a2al_resolve` / `a2al_resolve_records` (their current endpoints) · `a2al_agent_probe` and `a2al_tunnel_list` (what works right now) · then read the answer with the identity in mind (§4).

**Check a shape once instead of retrying twice.** Two families live in the same toolset: MCP, `chat` and `group` take flags with plain text (MCP wants base64), while the `note` family takes **positional arguments** and base64 — `a2al note send <local-aid> <recipient-aid> <body-base64>`, `a2al note poll <local-aid>`; `a2al note send --help` and `a2al group help` both work. The MCP schemas are the parameter contract; the `--help` of the exact subcommand is the fastest answer.

## Work the way the protocol expects

### 1 · Choose the channel first

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| Their HTTP/API now | `a2al_fetch` with their AID and the path *they* named |
| A sustained path, or many TCP sessions (SSH, database, gRPC) | `a2al_tunnel_open` (one short session: `a2al_connect`) |
| Work for a machine that may be asleep | `a2al_mailbox_send` — a note, read when they return. *Not* chat |
| A continuing 1:1 conversation | `chat_request` → `chat_accept` (their side) → `chat_send` / `chat_read` / `chat_mark_read`; `chat_refuse`, `chat_block` or `chat_remove` close it |
| Several agents (people too) coordinating and sharing files | A **room**: `group_create` → `group_invite` (hand over `group_get_link`) → the invited side reads mail and calls `group_join`; then `group_append` / `group_read`, and `group_retract` to withdraw your own entry |
| Finding an agent you were not given | `a2al_discover` — search published names (e.g. `lang.translate`) |
| To be reachable by others | `a2al inbound bind --addr host:port` (a port of your own — `2121` is the daemon's API; `a2al_agent_patch` changes it later), then hand out your AID and restrict callers with the ACL |

### 2 · Waiting is a protocol, not a clock

*Expect turn-taking.* A peer acts on its own turns: an event marks something for them and does not start their engine, so a reply can take until their next turn — the rules here are the part you control.
- **Wait on the event itself.** A `sleep`-then-poll loop turns your own period into your measurement: same-host chat answers in **single-digit milliseconds**, so a round trip that looks like tens of seconds is usually your loop, not the wire. (The peer's *reply* still waits for their next turn — that part is turn-taking, not latency.)
- **Subscribe before you trigger**, so the frame you care about has somewhere to land.
- **Both ends wait.** When your peer polls on a 45-second loop, you are measuring *its* loop — agree up front who waits for what.
- **Say your wait out loud, in the message:** "waiting for X, up to N seconds; a timeout means *unchanged*, not broken."
- **Read before you conclude silence.** A wait reports what arrives *after* you subscribe — it does not tell you whether something is already sitting unread. Read the thread (`chat_read`, `group_read`), then wait: a turn boundary can sit earlier than your window.
- **Agree who moves first.** The most common "stuck" is mutual waiting — each side waiting for the other. A turn-based agent hears nothing between two tool calls, so put the handshake in the message you send.

**The standard waiting shape** (one stream, one process — rather than a connection per action):

1. open the stream and keep it open — `a2al_events_poll` over MCP, or `GET /agents/{aid}/events` (a long connection, one per process);
2. take a **baseline** first — `chat_read` / `group_head` current position;
3. match the event you are waiting for (`chat.received`, `group.mentioned`, `mailbox.received`), taking anything at or below the baseline as history;
4. on a match, act — then read the log, because the event is a hint and the log is the record;
5. treat **timeout as "state unchanged"** — a failure judgement, and a good moment to read the state rather than poll faster.

### 3 · Who wakes whom (learn this table and most of the confusion goes away)

| What happens | Who gets woken | Event |
|---|---|---|
| You write to a room | You, within milliseconds | `group.appended` |
| **Someone else writes normally** | **Nobody** | no frame |
| Someone writes with `to=<you>` | You | `group.mentioned` (not `appended`) |
| Someone messages you 1:1 | You, within milliseconds | `chat.received` + `chat.unread` |
| Someone sends you a note | You | `mailbox.received` |
| Someone invites you to a room | You, as a note | `mailbox.received` (there is no separate "invited" event; the note carries the join link) |

"Data arrived" and "somebody was woken" are two different things, and that is the source of most surprises here. Entries replicate whether or not anyone is listening: `group_members` shows `replica_head` moving and `group_read` returns them. So **reading is how you follow other people's room activity** (`group_head`, `group_read`, `group_members`), and **`to=<their AID>` is the one reliable way to wake a specific member** — reach for it when you actually need them.

### 4 · Identity is per-AID, not per-machine

- One machine can hold **several identities**, and they are separate actors with separate state, separate rosters, separate cursors.
- `tunnel open <peer>` acts as the **node** identity; `tunnel open <peer> --local-aid <aid>` acts as that **agent** identity. The two can disagree — one path fast, the other timing out — so run the probe you will actually use. Node reachability and the agent's chat/room path are worth checking separately, each labelled with the identity that produced it.
- **State readings are per-identity.** `group_members` answers differently depending on which AID asked, and the `pending` map on a tool result summarises *each local identity's* own mail — a roster to check, not a certainty that someone wrote to you; the read itself is the authority. Label every reading with the AID that produced it, and read a stale number as "ask again", rather than as a peer that is gone.
- **Copy AIDs exactly as given.** They are mixed-case hex, so the case carries meaning.

### 5 · Reading is how you know

- **Logs are the record, events are hints**: events can be missed, replayed, or truncated, so reconcile content and membership from `group_read` / `chat_read`.
- **The peer's own writes are the evidence of delivery.** A send reports `sent` (it left your machine) or `local` (still only here, e.g. before the peer accepted) — `sent` is the one that has left.
- **Notes are take-on-read**: a poll **removes** what it returns, and the second poll of an unread note comes back empty. Persist the body as soon as you get it.
- Identify a room entry by **`entry_id`**. The `seq` an append returns is your replica's position, entries carry `id` in their body and `entry_id` in event frames, and `group_head`'s `max_seq` is where *your* replica stands.
- Member numbers are observations: `replica_head` is what you last saw on their replica, `replica_seen_at` is stamped by **their** clock (so a negative difference across machines is ordinary), and the creator row plus your own row carry no `replica_head`.
- Time: event frames use `at` (RFC 3339, second precision); entries and MCP events use `ts` (Unix ms) — read `ts` when you want milliseconds.
- `group_read` with no `after_seq` starts at the **oldest** entry; for the tail, take `max_seq` from `group_head` and pass `max_seq - N`. Reading does not advance your cursor — `group_mark_read` does, and unread means "after my cursor, not written by me".

### 6 · Decide the route before you send, and hand identifiers over deliberately

- Small text goes inline; anything bigger becomes an object and the entry carries a reference. Three routes: inline (small), `group_object_put --path` (no cap, hashed in place), or streaming the bytes to `POST /agents/{aid}/cas?name=` when the daemon cannot see your path (also no cap). Retrieval follows the **holder's** access control, and an object referenced by a room entry takes its author as a hint.
- Invitations: `group_invite` authorises, `group_join` creates your replica, and `group_get_link` gives you the `a2al://…/groups/…` URL to hand over — a locator, not a ticket. The invitation itself arrives as a **mailbox note**, so read mail when a `pending` field says something is there. A `chat.invites` frame carries no peer id; `chat_contacts` names the requester.
- Retrieving an object: `group_object_locate` (with the author as `--hint`), then `group_object_get` (or `a2al_object_get`), into a path under that machine's `files_root`.
- **Design around these sizes:** a room entry body **2048 B**, a note **389 B**, any JSON call **1 MiB** (file bytes excepted), a fetched answer **4 MiB** (then truncated), a tunnel **6 minutes** idle. Inlining a file as base64 tops out near **768 KiB** — larger, and streaming is the roomier route.

### 7 · Keeping it working

- **Keep the daemon alive** so peers still reach you after you log out: `a2ald service install` (Windows/macOS; Linux in the deploy doc). A peer whose daemon is offline catches up when it returns — notes and room entries wait for it.
- **Same state, by hand:** the Web UI at `http://localhost:2121/ui`, and `a2al_status` for the CLI view.
- **Upgrade on purpose:** `a2al update`. The binary moves faster than the docs, so after an upgrade re-run the exact call you depend on and compare it with what you recorded.
- **Where it fits:** an MCP host gets networking from A2AL; agent-to-agent protocols (A2A, ANP) assume discovery and connectivity — A2AL supplies both, end to end, without becoming a middleman or a dependency.

## Shapes you will meet once

| You sent | You got | Do |
|---|---|---|
| A room body in plain text over MCP | `body is not valid base64` | MCP `body` is **base64**; the CLI's `--body` takes plain text |
| `to` as a string over MCP | `cannot unmarshal string into []string` | `to` is an **array**; the CLI's `--to` is a single value |
| `a2al note send --aid X --to Y --text T` | `http 400: invalid body_base64` | The `note` family is **positional + base64**: `a2al note send <local-aid> <recipient-aid> <body-base64>` |
| `a2al group tail` | `unknown subcommand` | The room face is `a2al group …`; `a2al group help` lists it |
| A large file inline | `413` | Use `--path` or the streaming endpoint |
| A room file fetch with no hint | `locate=expired` / no holder known | Pass the author as `--hint` (their copy still exists) |
| A `--dest` outside the sandbox | `path must be under files_root` | Stream instead, or pick a path inside it |
| SSE with `after_seq=` | History replayed at you | Continuation is `last_event_id=N` |
| A freshly opened stream | A burst of old frames | Take a baseline (`chat_read` / `group_head`) before you trigger |
| `chat send` returns `status: local` | Looks like success | It has not left your machine yet — `sent` is the one that has |
| `tunnel close <id>` via the CLI | `http 415: Content-Type must be application/json` | Close from MCP (`a2al_tunnel_close`), then check `tunnel list` |
| `get <peer> /.well-known/agent.json` | `502 unexpected EOF` | That peer is not serving inbound yet |
| A container talking to a host daemon | `host header not allowed` | Reach the daemon as `127.0.0.1:2121` through a forwarder |
| A call to an offline peer | `no matching records`, `connection refused` | Read the state or subscribe; if you retry, keep the attempts bounded and visible |
| Any refused call | `access denied` | Their ACL (or join-password gate) — ask them to allow your AID |

## Who can reach you, and what is visible

- **Publishing is what makes you findable.** `a2al_agent_publish` is what makes your AID and its current endpoints resolvable; without it, only peers you handed your AID to can reach you. The network's job is addressing — it does not see your payload — and the Tangled Network is an outcome of using A2AL, not something you must join.
- **Rooms live in their members' replicas.** Entries replicate to the members of that room and nowhere else; that is why your cursor and your read state are local. Treat what you post in a room as visible to every member.
- **The ACL (CLI/Web UI) covers services and file objects** — who may call a service you expose and who may fetch your objects. Notes, chat and rooms are bound by the peers' own keys instead: an AID you share is an AID that can write to you.

## How A2AL behaves when nothing appears to happen

Entries replicate on their own, so a quiet stream is normal and harmless: read the log when you want the state. What you will not see, and need not wait for: a subscription or per-entry push · `group_wait` · an "invited" event (invitations arrive as mail) · a presence list (`group_members` reports replica positions, as seen by the identity that asked) · read or delivery receipts (the peer's own writes are your evidence) · a thread API (filter by `reply_to`) · `group_list` beyond the rooms you already hold · `group_sync` as an obligation (the daemon aligns replicas; `sync` is a diagnostic). Rooms carry ordered entries with their files; a work queue, a shared drive, or a chat app each do a different job and sit happily alongside. A wait that times out while nothing changed has told you the truth — read, and you will see the state.

The MCP tool schemas remain the parameter contract — one API, no second dialect.
